query: How does incident resolution efficiency vary across category, priority, and assignment group?

per_column.name: resolution_time_hours
per_column.rationale: This is essentially the operationalization of resolution efficiency itself, not an external associational variable. It restates the focus and is too fine-grained to segment on for grouped comparison.

per_column.name: sla_met
per_column.rationale: A binary derived directly from resolution time versus SLA; it is another expression of efficiency/outcome rather than an independent explanatory dimension to compare efficiency against.

per_column.name: resolution_speed_category
per_column.rationale: A binned version of the focus. Interpretable categories, but it IS the focus discretized, not an external variable to segment against. Also heavily imbalanced ('Very Slow' 411/500).

per_column.name: category_avg_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: A group-level aggregate of the focus keyed to category (already present). It is a summary of the target, not an external associational variable, and is near-constant (181.43 for 406 rows).

per_column.name: assignment_group_avg_resolution_hours
per_column.rationale: Same issue: an aggregate of the focus keyed to an existing segmentation column. Near-constant dominant value; opaque restatement rather than an interpretable external segmentation.

per_column.name: resolution_vs_category_avg
per_column.rationale: A residual of the focus minus its category mean. Continuous, fine-grained, and derived purely from the target; not an external variable and not a clean segmentation.

judge.rationale: The query asks how efficiency varies across category, priority, and assignment group -- segmentation dimensions that already exist in the original table. Every added column is a derivative or restatement of the focus (raw time, SLA flag, speed bins, group averages of the target, residuals). None introduces a NEW external, interpretable associational variable to group on and compare efficiency against. Several are also near-constant or too fine-grained. As a set, they fail the exploratory-analysis claim of opening informative relationships around the focus.
